excerpt: Render is a San Francisco cloud platform for deploying web apps, APIs, background workers, databases and static sites without managing servers. Free tier, funding and alternatives.
content:
Render is a cloud application platform: developers connect a Git repository and Render builds and runs their code, handling servers, scaling, TLS certificates and deploys. It hosts web services, private services, background workers, cron jobs, static sites, managed PostgreSQL databases and a Redis-compatible key-value store. Its pitch, as SDxCentral summarised it, is to be a simpler and cheaper alternative to the big hyperscale clouds, and it says it is attracting workloads moving from AWS, Google Cloud and Azure.

Render's about page names Anurag Goel as founder and CEO, says the company is based in San Francisco with a remote team around the world, and puts total funding at $258 million. In January 2025 Render announced an $80 million Series C led by Georgian, with 01A and avra joining existing investors including Addition, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst and the South Park Commons Fund. At the time it said more than 2 million developers used the platform and more than 100,000 new developers joined each month, and that the money would go to enterprise features, AI-native compute infrastructure and global expansion.

Render has a free tier. According to its documentation, free web services spin down after 15 minutes without traffic and take about a minute to wake up; each workspace gets 750 free instance hours a month; and a free PostgreSQL database is capped at 1 GB and expires after 30 days unless upgraded. Paid instances are billed by the second according to instance size, with workspace plans that add team features. The pricing page also lists persistent disks at $0.25 per GB and 500 included build minutes a month before extra charges. Teams moving production infrastructure can apply for up to $10,000 in migration credits.

This page is research, not a review. We have not run production workloads on Render; facts come from its pages and the reporting under Sources.
